newsitem.title: UK: US consumer credit quality decline slows - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: US consumer credit quality decline slows - Moody's.

text.p: The pace of deterioration in U.S. consumer credit quality eased slightly in September, Moody's Investors Service data showed on Wednesday.

The chargeoff rate (which is defined as account balances written off as uncollectable, as an annualised percentage of total loans) rose to 5.59 percent in September 1996, up more than 30 percent from the 4.27 percent rate in September 1995.
That figure was the smallest increase since March 1996 and was the third consecutive monthly decline in the growth rate of that index, Moody's said in a statement.
For third quarter 1996 as a whole, the chargeoff rate averaged 5.57 percent, compared with 4.14 percent in third quarter 1995 and with 5.52 percent in second quarter 1996.
"The slowing pace in the chargeoff growth rate reflects tighter standards and strengthened collection efforts by credit card lenders since January 1996," said Ed Bankole, senior analyst at Moody's.
"Other factors contributing to the slowdown include the improving trend in real wages and employment, which should gradually ease the debt servicing burden on consumers."
Moody's said the delinquency rate in securitised pools of credit card receivables increased to 5.07 percent in September 1996 from 4.17 percent in September 1995.
That was the first time since February 1994 that the delinquency rate exceeded 5.0 percent and was also the eleventh consecutive year-over-year increase in the delinquency rate.
For the third quarter of 1996 as a whole, the delinquency rate averaged 4.87 percent, compared with 4.08 percent in third quarter 1995.

"Overall credit quality pressures may gradually abate, but current consumer financial pressures may cause both the chargeoff rate and the delinquency rate to remain high throughout 1996," Moody's said.
"Those pressures are evident in both the rising consumer bankruptcy filing rates and in the debt service burden ratios."
The debt service burden ratio measures the proportion of household income devoted to repaying consumer debt each month.
Mooyd's said that ratio reached 11.0 percent in March 1996, its highest level since at least 1975, and remained at that level in the second quarter of 1996.
